items.title: 15.3.1 Generation and Transmission of Nerve Impulse

source_refs.note: Topic 15.3.1 with its For Information and Tidbit boxes (PDF 30-32); Figures 15.4 and 15.5 (both printed as 15.5) are replaced by original diagrams, each placed with its own text.

blocks.text: 1 Before the impulse: resting membrane potential

A resting neuron, not carrying a signal, is polarized: negative inside and positive outside. Its membrane potential, the resting membrane potential (RMP), is about -70 millivolts; the minus sign means the inside is negative relative to the outside. Three factors set it up.

items: Fixed anions: large negatively charged molecules such as proteins and nucleic acids are more abundant inside the cell and cannot diffuse out.

The sodium-potassium pump: K+ is about 30 times more concentrated inside than outside and Na+ about 10 times more concentrated outside. Pumps in the membrane use ATP to move these ions against their gradients, three Na+ out for every two K+ in, so the inside becomes more negative.
K+ leakage: some K+ ions leak out through K+ gates. This exit of K+ and the retention of negatively charged proteins are the major factors for the RMP.

blocks.alt: A neuron drawn as a circle with its membrane. Inside are proteins and nucleic acids marked as fixed anions. An intracellular electrode inside the cell and an extracellular electrode outside lead to a meter scaled -70, 0 and +90. A Na-K pump in the membrane moves 3Na+ out and 2K+ in, and a dashed arrow shows K+ leakage out of the cell.

blocks.text: When a neuron becomes active, the membrane potential at one region reverses so that the inside becomes positive relative to the outside. This is the active membrane potential, or action potential, produced by these events.

items: Depolarization: Na+ gates open and Na+ rushes in, cancelling the negative charge inside; the potential goes from -70 mV through zero to +50 mV, on a short region for about one millisecond.
Repolarization: Na+ gates close and K+ gates open; K+ diffuses out and the inside becomes negative again.

Hyperpolarization: because the K+ gates are slow to close, the potential briefly goes a little more negative than the RMP. During hyperpolarization, the neuron cannot generate another action potential and this period is called the refractory period.
Return to RMP: the sodium-potassium pump restores the original ion distribution and the membrane returns to -70 mV, ready for the next action potential.
book_errors: the neuron cannot generate another action potential

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book says that during hyperpolarization the neuron cannot generate another action potential. In fact the absolute refractory period, when no stimulus can fire the neuron, covers depolarization and most of repolarization; during hyperpolarization (the relative refractory period) a new action potential can be generated, but only by a stronger-than-normal stimulus.

blocks.alt: Graph of membrane potential (-80 to +50 mV) against time. From the resting potential of -70 mV (1) the curve rises steeply (depolarization, Na+ flows in, 2) to +50 mV, the action potential, then falls (repolarization, K+ flows out, 3), dips slightly below -70 mV (hyperpolarization) and returns to the RMP (4). Four small membrane panels show the Na+ and K+ gates at stages 1 to 4.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.5: Generation of action potential (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 15.5).
blocks.long_description: Panel notes as printed: 1 At RMP, some K+ channels are open. 2 Rapid depolarization occurs because Na+ gates open, allowing Na+ to diffuse into. 3 K+ gates open, repolarization occurs due to the diffusion of K+ out. 4 Hyperpolarization occurs before membrane returns to its original RMP.

blocks.text: Action potentials do not really travel along the axon; they are reproduced at neighbouring regions. An action potential in one region acts as a depolarizing stimulus for the next, which produces its own action potential, while the previous region repolarizes back to the RMP.

blocks.alt: A neuron with an enlarged strip of its axon membrane shown at five moments, top to bottom. Each strip shows + and - charges on both sides of the membrane. First resting; then a region depolarizes as Na+ enters (the action potential); the depolarized region moves along while K+ leaves behind it; the region behind becomes hyperpolarized; finally the membrane returns to resting.
blocks.caption: Figure 15.5: Propagation of action potential (original drawing after the textbook's second Figure 15.5).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Cell membrane, Resting, Depolarization (Action potential), Hyperpolarization, Resting; Na+ and K+ arrows.

blocks.title: A stadium wave
blocks.text: Propagation is like a 'wave' in a stadium: each person stays in place, stands up (depolarizes), raises the hands (action potential) and sits down again (repolarizes), and the wave moves round.
